It is used for multi-field gradients because the gradient orientation may not correspond to the surface of the classified region and can flip direction [S5, unofficial].

The claim states that the method is used for multi-field gradients because gradient orientation may not correspond to the surface of the classified region and can flip direction. Source [S5] explicitly states: 'Furthermore, this orientation may not even correspond to the surface of the classified region. Our approach uses an atmospheric lighting model which does not rely on a surface normal... This lighting model simply attenuates light through the volume, providing simple but robust lighting.' The source confirms that the orientation issue (not corresponding to the surface) is a known problem and that the atmospheric lighting model (which does not rely on surface normals) is the solution used. While the specific phrase 'can flip direction' is not explicitly in the provided text snippet, the core justification regarding the orientation not corresponding to the surface and the use of a model that doesn't rely on surface normals is directly supported. The 'flip direction' aspect is often associated with the ambiguity of eigenvector orientation mentioned in the first sentence of the passage ('choice of eigenvector may not be clear'), which supports the general context of orientation instability. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim.
